name: Laryngotracheoesophageal Cleft Type 3

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Clinical and Endoscopic Diagnostic Criteria for Laryngotracheoesophageal Cleft

criteria.description: Direct endoscopic visualization of a cleft extending through the posterior larynx into the trachea and esophagus consistent with type 3 classification
Presence of recurrent aspiration, feeding difficulties, and respiratory distress in neonates or infants
Contrast esophagography demonstrating abnormal communication between the larynx, trachea, and esophagus
Identification of associated congenital anomalies such as tracheoesophageal fistula or cardiac defects

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: Definitive diagnosis requires direct endoscopic visualization of the cleft (major criterion) plus clinical presentation consistent with aspiration and feeding difficulties, supported by radiologic evidence.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis is often confirmed intraoperatively or via bronchoscopy and esophagoscopy.

pathognomonic.notes: Due to abnormal communication between airway and esophagus
searchTerms: recurrent pneumonia due to inhaled food or liquids

pathognomonic.notes: Resulting from impaired separation of airway and digestive tract
Indicative of airway compromise from cleft

occasional.notes: Due to airway obstruction or aspiration

rare.notes: May coexist as part of syndromic presentations

laboratory: Normal routine blood tests; possible elevated inflammatory markers during aspiration pneumonia
imaging: Contrast esophagography showing abnormal communication between larynx, trachea, and esophagus
Chest X-ray showing recurrent infiltrates consistent with aspiration pneumonia
CT or MRI may delineate extent of cleft and associated anomalies
genetic: No specific genetic mutation identified; may be associated with syndromes involving midline defects
other: Endoscopic bronchoscopy and esophagoscopy confirming cleft extent and classification

distinguishingFeatures: Presence of fistulous tract between trachea and esophagus without involvement of larynx
Different clinical presentation with less extensive airway involvement
Inspiratory stridor without aspiration or feeding difficulties
No abnormal communication between airway and esophagus

redFlags: Severe respiratory distress with cyanosis during feeding
Recurrent aspiration pneumonia despite standard management
Failure to thrive with persistent feeding intolerance
references: Holinger LD. Laryngotracheoesophageal clefts: a review of 12 cases. Laryngoscope. 1989.
Smith MM, et al. Diagnosis and management of laryngotracheoesophageal clefts. Int J Pediatr Otorhinolaryngol. 2015.
